documents.title: Introduction to DBMS
documents.definition_text:
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that allows users and applications to create, store, organize, retrieve, update and manage data in a database.

It acts as an interface between users and the database. When a user requests information, the DBMS processes that request, communicates with the database and returns the required result.

A DBMS also provides important facilities such as data security, access control, data integrity, backup and recovery, and transaction management. These facilities help ensure that data remains accurate, protected and available to authorized users.

Examples of DBMS software include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database and SQLite.
documents.example_text: Spotify uses a DBMS to link millions of tracks, playlists, and user listening histories.

documents.title: History of DBMS
documents.summary: Trace the evolution from 1960s Hierarchical and Network models to Codd’s Relational Model and modern Cloud/NoSQL systems.
documents.definition_text: DBMS technology evolved from rigid 1960s Navigational databases (Hierarchical IMS & Network CODASYL) to Edgar F. Codd’s 1970 Relational Model (tables + SQL), followed by Object-Relational, NoSQL, and distributed cloud databases.
documents.example_text: Before 1970, programmers wrote complex pointer-chasing code to walk tree paths. Codd’s Relational Model let anyone ask "what" they wanted with SQL instead of "how" to navigate pointers.

documents.title: Advantages of DBMS
documents.summary: Explore how DBMS reduces redundancy, prevents inconsistency, enforces security, and supports concurrent backups.
documents.definition_text: Key advantages of a DBMS include controlling data redundancy, guaranteeing data consistency, enforcing integrity constraints, providing fine-grained security, enabling concurrent multi-user access, and automating crash backup and recovery.
documents.example_text: When a student updates their email once in the Students table, admissions, library, and exam portals all see the updated email instantly.

documents.practical_explanation: Centralized storage allows fast, accurate company-wide analytics and sharing.

documents.title: Disadvantages of DBMS
documents.summary: Evaluate DBMS trade-offs: hardware/licensing costs, complexity, DBA staffing, and single-point-of-failure risks.
documents.definition_text: Despite its strengths, a DBMS introduces notable trade-offs: high software/hardware cost, setup and maintenance complexity, specialized Database Administrator (DBA) training needs, performance overhead for tiny apps, and higher impact if a centralized server fails.
documents.example_text: Running an enterprise Oracle cluster just to store a 10-line configuration file wastes memory, money, and setup time compared to a simple JSON/text file.

documents.title: Need for DBMS
documents.summary: Understand the concrete technical problems—scale, concurrency, crash safety, and ad-hoc querying—that make DBMS indispensable.
documents.definition_text: Organizations need a DBMS because manual file code breaks down when data grows beyond memory, when hundreds of users edit simultaneously, when queries change unexpectedly (ad-hoc queries), or when sudden crashes threaten partial writes.
documents.example_text: If a sudden report asks for "CS students with GPA > 3.7 who took CS301", a DBMS answers in 1 SQL line, whereas custom file scripts would require writing and compiling new search code.

The moment 500 users need fast, crash-safe answers at the same time, you need a DBMS.","detailedExplanation":"There are five core reasons modern software needs a DBMS: (1) Persistent Scale—managing gigabytes or terabytes far larger than RAM; (2) Concurrent Access—letting many users read and write without corrupting bytes; (3) Ad-hoc Querying—answering unpredictable questions quickly in SQL; (4) Security & Privacy—controlling exactly who sees which columns; and (5) Crash Recovery—guaranteeing partial operations roll back cleanly.","definitions":[{"term":"Ad-hoc Query","meaning":"An unscheduled, on-the-fly question posed to a database without writing new application code."},{"term":"Lost Update","meaning":"Concurrency bug where two simultaneous edits overwrite one another."}],"realWorldExamples":["A dean asks for the top 3 GPAs per department 5 minutes before a meeting—SQL answers immediately.","If a payment server reboots mid-checkout, DBMS recovery rolls back incomplete charges."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Instant Ad-Hoc Ranking","snippet":"SELECT full_name, gpa FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.8 ORDER BY gpa DESC;","outcome":"Delivers sorted honors list in under a millisecond."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"01","title":"Scale Beyond RAM","detail":"Page buffers & indexes handle huge datasets."},{"step":"02","title":"Coordinate Users","detail":"Locks stop simultaneous writers from clashing."},{"step":"03","title":"Survive Crashes","detail":"Logs undo half-finished writes on restart."}],"commonMistakes":["Assuming \"saving to a JSON file\" scales to multi-user web apps—concurrent writes to plain files easily corrupt data."],"quickRecap":["We need DBMS for scale, ad-hoc querying, concurrency safety, access control, and crash recovery."]}

documents.title: Introduction to DBMS Architecture
documents.summary: See how clients, query processors, storage engines, and tier levels fit together inside a DBMS.
documents.definition_text: DBMS Architecture defines how users, application servers, query processors, and physical storage interact. Depending on deployment needs, DBMS systems are structured across 1-Tier (1-Level), 2-Tier (2-Level), or 3-Tier (3-Level) architectures.
documents.example_text: In a web app like DBMS Arena, your browser talks to an Express API server, which talks to the SQLite/SQL engine—a classic multi-level architecture.
documents.diagram_config_json: {"layers":[{"id":"client","label":"Presentation / Client Layer","role":"UI, dashboards, and query forms","sample":"Browser / Mobile App"},{"id":"app","label":"Application / Query Layer","role":"Business rules, authentication & query optimization","sample":"API Server + Query Optimizer"},{"id":"data","label":"Database Storage Layer","role":"Tables, indexes, buffer manager & transaction logs","sample":"SQL Engine + Disk Pages"}]}
documents.practical_sql: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';
documents.practical_explanation: The DBMS catalog stores metadata describing every table managed inside the architecture.
documents.lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"Just like a building has a blueprint separating plumbing, electrical wiring, and living rooms, a DBMS uses layered architecture to separate user screens from raw disk storage.","detailedExplanation":"DBMS architecture can be viewed in two complementary ways: deployment tiers (1-Level, 2-Level, 3-Level client/server separation) and internal schema abstraction (External, Conceptual, Internal). Separating layers improves security (browsers never directly touch raw disk files), scalability (multiple web servers can share one database cluster), and maintainability.","definitions":[{"term":"DBMS Architecture","meaning":"Structural blueprint governing how clients, business logic, and database storage communicate."},{"term":"Query Processor","meaning":"DBMS component that parses SQL, optimizes execution plans, and fetches rows."}],"realWorldExamples":["ATM -> Bank Middleware Server -> Core Banking Database.","Browser -> Node.js Express Backend -> SQLite/PostgreSQL Engine."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Inspecting System Catalog","snippet":"SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table';","outcome":"Queries the internal metadata layer of the database architecture."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"01","title":"1-Level","detail":"User + DBMS + Files on one machine."},{"step":"02","title":"2-Level","detail":"Client UI talks directly to DB Server over API/ODBC."},{"step":"03","title":"3-Level","detail":"Client -> App Server -> DB Server (modern web standard)."}],"commonMistakes":["Mixing up 1/2/3-Tier physical deployment architecture with the ANSI-SPARC 3-Schema logical abstraction—both use \"3-Level\" terminology in textbooks!"],"quickRecap":["DBMS Architecture separates presentation, query/business logic, and physical storage across 1, 2, or 3 levels."]}

documents.title: 1-Level Architecture
documents.summary: Examine single-tier architecture where user interface, DBMS engine, and disk files live on one machine.
documents.definition_text: In 1-Level (1-Tier) Architecture, the database engine, storage files, and user interface all reside on the exact same computer. Changes made by the user go directly to the local database without network hops.
documents.example_text: A developer running SQLite locally inside a desktop app or practicing SQL directly on a single workstation uses 1-Level Architecture.
documents.diagram_config_json: {"layers":[{"id":"single","label":"Single Machine (1-Tier)","role":"UI + Business Logic + DBMS + Disk File all in one process","sample":"Local App -> local_db.sqlite (Zero network latency)"}]}
documents.practical_sql: SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects;
documents.practical_explanation: Local embedded SQLite queries execute directly against local memory/disk with sub-millisecond latency.
documents.lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"Have you ever used a mobile app that works offline on an airplane? Its local database lives right inside your phone—that is 1-Level Architecture.","detailedExplanation":"In 1-Level Architecture, there is no network separation between the user interface and the database server. Everything runs locally on a single machine. This makes setup effortless and latency nearly zero, which is ideal for local development, embedded devices, and single-user tools. However, it cannot easily share live data across hundreds of remote users simultaneously.","definitions":[{"term":"1-Level (1-Tier) Architecture","meaning":"All-in-one architecture where client UI and DBMS run directly on the same host machine."},{"term":"Embedded Database","meaning":"A lightweight DBMS library (like SQLite) compiled directly inside an application."}],"realWorldExamples":["Mobile apps storing offline notes or contacts in an embedded SQLite file.","A student running a local MySQL workbench directly on their laptop for assignments."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Local Embedded Query","snippet":"SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects;","outcome":"Runs locally in < 1 ms without network round-trips."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"01","title":"Local Request","detail":"App calls DBMS library function directly."},{"step":"02","title":"Direct Disk Read","detail":"Engine reads local database file immediately."}],"commonMistakes":["Trying to scale a 1-tier local file app directly to thousands of concurrent internet users—multi-user web apps need 2-tier or 3-tier architectures."],"quickRecap":["1-Level Architecture = UI + DBMS + Storage on one machine; super fast and simple, best for local/offline apps."]}

documents.title: 2-Level Architecture
documents.summary: Learn Client-Server 2-Tier architecture using JDBC/ODBC APIs between client workstations and a central DB server.
documents.definition_text: In 2-Level (2-Tier) Architecture, Client machines run the user interface and application logic while communicating directly over a network with a centralized Database Server using standard drivers like JDBC or ODBC.
documents.example_text: A desktop bank teller app in a branch sends SQL queries directly over an internal network to the branch’s central PostgreSQL server.

documents.practical_explanation: In 2-Tier setups, client apps send SQL statements straight to the DB server and receive result tables.
documents.lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"Once a team needs multiple computers to share the same live data, we split the app into two parts: client workstations (Tier 1) and a central database server (Tier 2).","detailedExplanation":"2-Level Architecture follows the classic Client-Server model. Tier 1 (Client) presents the UI and formats requests; Tier 2 (Database Server) stores data and runs queries. Standard APIs like ODBC and JDBC bridge the client to the database server. While easy to build for small internal teams, exposing direct database connections to thousands of public internet users creates security and connection-limit bottlenecks.","definitions":[{"term":"2-Level (2-Tier) Architecture","meaning":"Client-server design where client apps connect directly to the DBMS server over a network."},{"term":"JDBC / ODBC","meaning":"Standard database connectivity drivers allowing apps to send SQL directly to a DBMS."}],"realWorldExamples":["A desktop pharmacy POS terminal querying a back-office SQL Server machine.","An internal BI tool (like Tableau) connecting via ODBC to a company data warehouse."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Direct Client-to-Server Query","snippet":"SELECT instructor_id, full_name, dept_id FROM instructors;","outcome":"Client receives rows directly over the network socket."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"Tier 1","title":"Client Application","detail":"Builds UI and sends SQL via JDBC/ODBC."},{"step":"Tier 2","title":"Database Server","detail":"Authenticates, executes SQL, returns rows."}],"commonMistakes":["Exposing a 2-tier database port directly to public web browsers—browsers should always go through a 3rd Application Server tier."],"quickRecap":["2-Level = Client (UI) <-> Database Server via JDBC/ODBC; great for internal LAN apps, limited for huge public web scale."]}

documents.title: 3-Level Architecture
documents.summary: Master both 3-Tier web architecture (Client -> App Server -> DB) and ANSI-SPARC 3-Schema abstraction (External, Conceptual, Internal).
documents.definition_text: 3-Level Architecture covers two foundational concepts: (1) 3-Tier deployment (Client -> Application Server -> Database Server for web security and scale) and (2) the ANSI-SPARC 3-Schema Architecture separating External Level (views), Conceptual Level (logical tables), and Internal Level (physical disk blocks) to achieve Data Independence.
documents.example_text: DBMS Arena uses 3-Tier deployment (React Browser -> Express Server -> SQLite DB) AND 3-Schema abstraction (Student views vs conceptual tables vs B-tree disk pages).
documents.diagram_config_json: {"layers":[{"id":"ext","label":"External Level / Client Tier","role":"User-specific views & web UI (hides private columns)","sample":"VIEW PublicStudents AS SELECT full_name, dept_id FROM students;"},{"id":"con","label":"Conceptual Level / App Tier","role":"Logical database schema & business rules","sample":"students(student_id PK, full_name, email, dept_id FK, gpa)"},{"id":"int","label":"Internal Level / DB Storage Tier","role":"Physical disk pages, B+ trees & compression","sample":"Data blocks & index pages on SSD"}]}

documents.practical_explanation: Querying conceptual columns works seamlessly regardless of how the Internal physical storage is organized.
documents.lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"Why do modern apps put a middle layer between your browser and the database? And why can engineers reorganize disk storage without breaking existing SQL queries? The answer is 3-Level Architecture.","detailedExplanation":"In 3-Tier deployment, the Client (browser) talks only to an Application Server (middle tier), which validates permissions and queries the Database Server—preventing direct DB exposure. Meanwhile, the ANSI-SPARC 3-Schema Architecture splits database design into three levels: External (customized user views), Conceptual (the entire logical schema of tables and constraints), and Internal (physical disk files and indexes). This separation delivers Physical Data Independence (changing storage does not break tables) and Logical Data Independence (changing tables does not break user views).","definitions":[{"term":"External Level","meaning":"Top view layer tailored for specific user roles."},{"term":"Conceptual Level","meaning":"Middle logical layer describing all entities, types, and constraints."},{"term":"Internal Level","meaning":"Lowest physical layer describing disk blocks, pointers, and indexes."},{"term":"Data Independence","meaning":"Ability to modify a lower schema level without breaking higher levels."}],"realWorldExamples":["Every modern SaaS web app: Browser (Tier 1) -> Node/Python API (Tier 2) -> Postgres/SQLite (Tier 3).","Adding an SSD index at the Internal Level speeds up queries without changing any Conceptual SQL."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"External Projection View","snippet":"SELECT student_id, full_name, year_level FROM students;","outcome":"Exposes only safe columns to the External layer."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"Level 1","title":"External / Presentation","detail":"User views & browser interface."},{"step":"Level 2","title":"Conceptual / Application","detail":"Logical tables, constraints & API logic."},{"step":"Level 3","title":"Internal / Storage","detail":"Physical disk files, indexes & logs."}],"commonMistakes":["Confusing Physical Data Independence (Internal changes do not affect Conceptual) with Logical Data Independence (Conceptual changes do not affect External views)."],"quickRecap":["3-Level Architecture delivers security, scalability, and Physical/Logical Data Independence."]}

documents.title: Difference between File System and DBMS
documents.summary: Compare traditional OS file systems against DBMS across redundancy, concurrency, security, and query power.
documents.definition_text: A File System (like CSV/text files in folders) relies on custom application code to parse bytes and struggles with redundancy, inconsistency, weak security, and concurrent edits. A DBMS centralizes data with declarative SQL queries, ACID safety, and automatic indexing.
documents.example_text: If Registrar and Hostel departments store separate student.csv files, changing a phone number in one leaves the other outdated. A DBMS stores it once.

documents.title: Entity Relationship (ER) Model
documents.summary: Design high-level conceptual database blueprints using Peter Chen’s ER Model before writing any SQL.
documents.definition_text: Proposed by Peter Chen in 1976, the Entity Relationship (ER) Model is a high-level visual conceptual data model that represents real-world objects as Entities (rectangles), their properties as Attributes (ellipses), and associations between them as Relationships (diamonds).
documents.example_text: Before writing CREATE TABLE statements for a university, architects sketch Student, Course, and Instructor rectangles connected by Enrolls and Teaches diamonds.

documents.title: ER Entities & Attributes
documents.summary: Distinguish Strong vs Weak entities and Simple, Composite, Multivalued, Derived, and Key attributes.
documents.definition_text: In the ER Model, a Strong Entity has its own unique Key Attribute, whereas a Weak Entity (double rectangle) depends on an owner entity. Attributes come in five flavors: Simple (atomic), Composite (sub-parts like First + Last name), Single-valued vs Multivalued (double ellipse, e.g., phone numbers), Derived (dashed ellipse, e.g., Age from DOB), and Key Attributes (underlined).
documents.example_text: In Student, student_id is a Key attribute, full_name is Composite (first + last), phone_numbers is Multivalued, and age is Derived from birth_date.

Strong entities stand independently using their own Primary Key. Weak entities (such as an employee’s Dependent or an OrderLineItem) have no full key of their own and borrow their owner’s key. Attributes describe entities: Simple attributes cannot be split (gpa); Composite attributes break down (address -> street, city, zip); Multivalued attributes hold multiple values (skills); Derived attributes are computed from stored fields (age from DOB).","definitions":[{"term":"Strong Entity","meaning":"Independent entity set possessing its own Primary Key."},{"term":"Weak Entity","meaning":"Dependent entity identified only when paired with an owner entity’s key."},{"term":"Derived Attribute","meaning":"Value calculated dynamically from another stored attribute (e.g., age)."}],"realWorldExamples":["An InvoiceItem is a Weak Entity because \"Line #1\" only makes sense inside Invoice #402."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Inspecting Key & Simple Attributes","snippet":"SELECT student_id, full_name, email FROM students;","outcome":"Uses key attribute student_id and atomic email."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"Key","title":"Underlined Ellipse","detail":"Uniquely identifies each entity instance."},{"step":"Composite","title":"Branching Ellipses","detail":"Splits into sub-attributes."},{"step":"Derived","title":"Dashed Ellipse","detail":"Computed at query time, not stored."}],"commonMistakes":["Storing derived attributes like Age directly as static numbers—they become wrong after every birthday!"],"quickRecap":["Entities: Strong vs Weak. documents.title: ER Relationships & Cardinality
documents.summary: Model 1:1, 1:N, and M:N cardinality ratios and Total vs Partial participation in ER diagrams.
documents.definition_text: Cardinality Ratio defines how many instances of Entity A can link to Entity B: One-to-One (1:1), One-to-Many (1:N), or Many-to-Many (M:N). Participation Constraints define whether involvement is mandatory (Total Participation, double line) or optional (Partial Participation, single line).
documents.example_text: Department to Student is 1:N (one department has many students; each student belongs to one department). Student to Course is M:N (many students take many courses).
documents.diagram_config_json: {"scenarios":[{"id":"c1","left":"Department","rel":"Chaired By","right":"Instructor","ratio":"1 : 1","note":"Each department has 1 chair; an instructor chairs at most 1 department."},{"id":"c2","left":"Department","rel":"Enrolls","right":"Student","ratio":"1 : N","note":"1 department has many students; each student belongs to 1 department."},{"id":"c3","left":"Student","rel":"Takes","right":"Course","ratio":"M : N","note":"Students take multiple courses and courses hold multiple students."}]}

documents.practical_explanation: Counts the N-side Students linked to each 1-side Department.

Is a course required or optional?","detailedExplanation":"Cardinality limits maximum links: 1:1 (e.g., Country <-> Capital), 1:N (Department <-> Students), and M:N (Students <-> Courses). Participation limits minimum links: Total Participation (minimum 1—drawn with a double line) means every entity must participate (every Course must belong to a Department); Partial Participation (minimum 0—single line) means participation is optional (an Instructor might not chair any department).","definitions":[{"term":"Cardinality Ratio","meaning":"Maximum number of relationship instances (1:1, 1:N, M:N) an entity can join."},{"term":"Total Participation","meaning":"Mandatory rule where every entity instance must participate (double line)."},{"term":"Partial Participation","meaning":"Optional participation where some entities may remain unlinked (single line)."}],"realWorldExamples":["1:1: Passport <-> Citizen.","1:N: Author <-> Books.","M:N: Actors <-> Movies."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"Verifying 1:N Cardinality","snippet":"SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(s.student_id) AS student_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN students s ON d.dept_id = s.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id;","outcome":"Shows multiple students grouped under each department."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"1:1","title":"Exclusive Pair","detail":"Max 1 link on both sides."},{"step":"1:N","title":"Parent to Children","detail":"1 parent links to many children."},{"step":"M:N","title":"Mesh Association","detail":"Many-to-many solved via a junction table."}],"commonMistakes":["Confusing Cardinality (maximum: 1 or N) with Participation (minimum: optional partial vs mandatory total)."],"quickRecap":["Cardinality: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. documents.title: RDBMS (Relational Database Management System)
documents.summary: Understand how an RDBMS organizes data into tables (relations), rows (tuples), and columns (attributes).
documents.definition_text: RDBMS: A DBMS based on the relational model storing data in tables (relations) linked by Primary and Foreign Keys. A Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) implements E.F. Codd’s relational model. Every table is a Relation, every column is an Attribute with a fixed data type, and every row is a Tuple uniquely identified by a Primary Key. Foreign Keys link tables cleanly without repeating information.
documents.example_text: MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and SQLite are all RDBMS engines. Example: SELECT d.dept_name, s.full_name FROM students s JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id LIMIT 5;

documents.definition_text: DQL / DML / DDL: DQL queries rows (SELECT); DML modifies rows (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE); DDL defines structures (CREATE/ALTER/DROP). documents.definition_text: INNER JOIN: Join returning only rows that have matching key values in both tables. `SELECT ... documents.title: SQL LEFT JOIN

documents.definition_text: LEFT (OUTER) JOIN: Returns all rows from the left table plus matched rows from the right table (NULL when unmatched). `A LEFT JOIN B ON A.key = B.key` preserves every row from the left table `A`. documents.title: SQL HAVING
documents.summary: Filter grouped aggregate buckets AFTER GROUP BY runs, unlike WHERE which filters rows beforehand.
documents.definition_text: HAVING Clause: Group-level filter evaluated after GROUP BY and aggregate calculations. SQL executes `WHERE` first on individual rows, then `GROUP BY` creates buckets, and finally `HAVING` filters out buckets that fail an aggregate condition (like `HAVING AVG(gpa) > 3.7`).

Execution Outcome","role":"Keeps only departments with 2 or more students.","sample":"WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation."}]}

documents.title: SQL EXISTS
documents.summary: Test efficiently whether a correlated subquery returns at least one matching row using EXISTS.
documents.definition_text: EXISTS Operator: Boolean predicate returning TRUE if a subquery yields at least one row. `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE ...)` returns TRUE if the subquery produces one or more rows, and FALSE if it returns zero rows. Because it short-circuits on the first match, EXISTS is often faster than IN on large tables.

documents.title: SQL ANY Operator
documents.summary: Compare a value against a subquery list so the condition passes if true for AT LEAST ONE returned value.
documents.definition_text: ANY / SOME Operator: Subquery comparison returning TRUE if the comparison holds for at least one value returned by the subquery. `value > ANY (SELECT ...)` evaluates to TRUE if `value` is greater than at least one item in the subquery (equivalent to being greater than the minimum value). Note: In SQLite (used in our practice engine), `> ANY (subquery)` is written equivalently as `> (SELECT MIN(...) FROM ...)` or `EXISTS`.

documents.title: SQL ALL Operator

documents.definition_text: Relational Algebra: Procedural formal language defining algebraic operators that map input relations to a new output relation. documents.title: Selection (σ) and Projection (π)
documents.summary: Master unary operators Selection σ (horizontal row filter) and Projection π (vertical column filter).
documents.definition_text: Selection (σ) & Projection (π): σ filters rows by condition; π picks columns and eliminates duplicate rows. Selection `σ_p(R)` keeps tuples in relation `R` that satisfy predicate `p` (equivalent to SQL `WHERE`). Projection `π_A1,A2(R)` extracts only columns `A1, A2` and automatically removes duplicate tuples because relations are sets (equivalent to `SELECT DISTINCT`).
documents.example_text: `π_full_name(σ_dept_id="CS"(students))` finds names of all CS students. Example: SELECT DISTINCT full_name FROM students WHERE dept_id = 'CS';

documents.title: Relational Algebra Set Operations (∪, ∩, −, ×)
documents.summary: Combine union-compatible relations using Union (∪), Intersection (∩), Set Difference (−), and Cartesian Product (×).
documents.definition_text: Set Operations (∪, ∩, −, ×): Union, Intersection, Difference (on union-compatible tables) and Cartesian Product. Union (`R ∪ S`), Intersection (`R ∩ S`), and Set Difference (`R − S`) require `R` and `S` to be union-compatible (same degree/columns and compatible domains). Cartesian Product (`R × S`) pairs every tuple in `R` with every tuple in `S` without needing union-compatibility.

documents.definition_text: Natural Join (⋈) & Theta Join (⋈_θ): Binary operator combining related tuples across two tables based on a join condition or shared column names. documents.definition_text: Division (R ÷ S): Derived operator finding X values associated with ALL Y values in divisor relation S. Division `R(X, Y) ÷ S(Y)` returns every `X` value in `R` that is paired with EVERY `Y` value in `S`. In SQL, Division is commonly expressed using double-negation (`NOT EXISTS ... documents.summary: Understand exact set-based meaning, schema output types, and query equivalence rules.
documents.definition_text: Relational Semantics & Equivalence: Exact mathematical meaning of an algebraic expression and laws proving two expressions yield identical outputs. Semantics defines what an expression actually computes: (1) output schema (attribute names & types), and (2) output set of tuples. Because Relational Algebra is set-based, duplicate rows are eliminated. Semantic equivalence laws (such as Pushing Selection down before Join: `σ_p(R ⋈ S) ≡ σ_p(R) ⋈ S`) let optimizers run queries 100× faster without changing the answer.

documents.title: Relational Algebra Operators (Fundamental vs Derived)
documents.summary: Classify the 5–6 fundamental operators vs convenient derived shorthand operators.
documents.definition_text: Fundamental vs Derived Operators: Primitives {σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ} are irreducible; {∩, ⋈, ÷} are convenient combinations of primitives. The 5 fundamental (primitive) operators of Relational Algebra are: Selection (`σ`), Projection (`π`), Union (`∪`), Set Difference (`−`), and Cartesian Product (`×`) (plus Renaming `ρ`). Every other operator—Intersection (`R ∩ S = R − (R − S)`), Joins (`⋈`), and Division (`÷`)—is Derived from those primitives.
documents.example_text: Expressing Intersection without `∩`: `R ∩ S ≡ R − (R − S)`. Example: SELECT dept_id FROM students INTERSECT SELECT dept_id FROM projects;

documents.title: Extended Algebra: Grouping (γ) and Ungrouping
documents.summary: Extend Relational Algebra with Grouping/Aggregation (γ) and Nest/Unnest (Ungrouping) for structured data.
documents.definition_text: Grouping (γ) & Ungrouping: Grouping aggregates tuples by key (or nests sub-rows); Ungrouping flattens nested sets back into atomic tuples. The Grouping operator `γ_G;F(R)` groups tuples by attributes `G` and computes aggregate functions `F` (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX)—matching SQL `GROUP BY`. In nested relational models, Grouping (Nest) packs related sub-tuples into a relation-valued attribute, while Ungrouping (Unnest) flattens nested collections back into standard flat 1NF rows.
documents.example_text: `γ_dept_id; AVG(gpa)(students)` computes per-department average GPA. Example: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS count_students, ROUND(AVG(gpa), 2) AS avg_gpa FROM students GROUP BY dept_id;

documents.summary: Compare Relational Algebra, Tuple/Domain Relational Calculus, and SQL in expressive power and style.
documents.definition_text: Relational Completeness (Codd’s Theorem): Any query expressible in Safe Relational Calculus can be expressed in Relational Algebra, and vice versa. Practical SQL extends both with grouping, sorting, arithmetic, and updates.

documents.definition_text: Database Transaction: Logical unit of work moving a database from one consistent state to another via COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A Transaction is a sequence of database reads/writes treated as a single indivisible unit of work (`BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`). Its lifecycle moves from Active -> Partially Committed -> Committed (durable), or Failed -> Aborted (rolled back cleanly).

documents.definition_text: Normalization & Functional Dependency (X -> Y): Schema refinement decomposing tables using functional dependencies to remove redundancy and anomalies. Normalization is the systematic process of structuring relational tables to remove data redundancy and prevent Insertion, Update, and Deletion Anomalies. documents.definition_text: Second Normal Form (2NF): 1NF relation where no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key. A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if it is in 1NF AND has NO Partial Dependencies—meaning every non-prime attribute must be fully functionally dependent on the ENTIRE candidate key, not just a proper subset of a composite key. documents.title: Third Normal Form (3NF)
documents.summary: Eliminate Transitive Dependencies (A -> B -> C) so non-key attributes depend directly on the key and nothing else.
documents.definition_text: Third Normal Form (3NF): 2NF relation with no transitive dependencies between non-prime attributes. A relation is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if it is in 2NF AND has NO Transitive Dependencies—where a non-prime attribute determines another non-prime attribute (`student_id -> dept_id -> dept_building`). Moving `(dept_id, dept_building)` to `Departments` achieves 3NF.
documents.example_text: Moving `dept_name` and `building` out of `Students` into `Departments` removes `student_id -> dept_id -> building`. Example: SELECT dept_id, dept_name, building FROM departments;

documents.title: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
documents.summary: Enforce the strictest determinant rule: for every non-trivial X -> Y, X MUST be a Superkey.
documents.definition_text: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF): Strict normal form requiring every non-trivial determinant X (in X -> Y) to be a Superkey. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) strengthens 3NF with one crisp rule: for EVERY non-trivial functional dependency `X -> Y` holding in relation `R`, `X` MUST be a Superkey of `R`. Every BCNF table is guaranteed to be in 3NF, though a few 3NF schemas violate BCNF when overlapping candidate keys exist.
documents.example_text: If a course has multiple instructors and each instructor teaches only one course (`instructor -> course`), `instructor` must be made a superkey in its own decomposed table. Example: SELECT instructor_id, full_name, dept_id FROM instructors;
